**Question:** which proposed arrow actually explains amide electron
availability while conserving atoms, charge and ordinary valence?

Allow **10 minutes**: predict for 2, audit several moves for 5, then draw and
explain your corrected result for 3.

### Predict

Compare ethylamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂, with ethanamide, CH₃C(=O)NH₂. For the amide,
a nitrogen pair can form C=N only if the C=O pi pair moves to O at the same
time. Predict the O and N charges and the net charge in that contributor.

A full-headed arrow starts at a lone pair or bond. A positive-charge symbol
is not a pair source. Ordinary carbon must retain a total bond order of four.

### Explore

1. Select **Nitrogen lone pair → C–N pi bond** for the amide. Omit the coupled
   carbonyl move, inspect the feedback, and then include it.
2. Compare the same proposed move for ethylamine. Identify the missing
   neighbouring structural feature.
3. Try **Carbonyl pi pair → oxygen**. Distinguish this polar contributor from
   the coupled N-donation contributor.
4. Compare **formal amine protonation**. Explain why adding H⁺ changes a
   molecular species whereas drawing resonance contributors does not.

### Explain and check

The coupled amide contributor has **N⁺ and O⁻**, net zero:
CH₃C(=O)NH₂ ↔ CH₃C(O⁻)=NH₂⁺. The double-headed resonance link connects
representations of **one delocalised molecule**, not two species switching at
equilibrium. Partial C–N double-bond character helps explain restricted
rotation and altered N-pair availability.

Moving only the carbonyl pi pair gives a minor C⁺/O⁻ polar contributor; it
preserves net charge but does not alone show N donation. The tool distinguishes
formally valid accounting from the most useful or most stabilised contributor.

### Model limits

H⁺ abbreviates an actual proton donor; a complete reaction mechanism also
shows the donor bond breaking. Amide N protonation is possible as a formal
reaction but is much less favourable than ordinary alkylamine protonation;
under common strong-acid conditions amide O protonation can be preferred.
This tool does not compute site populations or energies. Use the local
[amide exercises](../acyl-chemistry/exercise.qmd) and
[nitrogen exercises](../amines-aromatics/exercise.qmd) for further practice.
